lede: A rope that pulls at an angle is doing two jobs at once: dragging along the floor and lifting. Resolving splits one slanted force into those two straight ones, so the rest of the mechanics can be done a direction at a time.
can: Split a force at an angle into a component along a line and one at right angles to it
Resolve the weight of a body on a slope into its two components
Read which angle to use, and which line it is measured from

md: Pull a suitcase by its handle and some of your pull drags it forwards while some lifts it. Splitting that one pull into a forwards part and an upwards part is what resolving does.

caption: One slanted pull replaced by two at right angles.

md: Drop a dashed line from the tip of the force onto the line you care about. The force is now the longest side of a right-angled triangle, and the two shorter sides are its components: the side beside the angle uses cosine, the side opposite uses sine.

**Along the floor:** $46\cos 22° = 42.65$ N, the side beside the angle.
**Upwards:** $46\sin 22° = 17.23$ N, the side opposite it.

prompt: A rope pulls a sledge with a force of 25 N at 40° to the ground. What is the part of the pull along the ground, in newtons, to 2 decimal places?
explain: The ground is beside the $40°$ angle, so it takes the cosine, as the floor did above: $25\cos 40° = 19.15$ N. The sine would give the part lifting the sledge.

text: 2. Why cosine goes with the angle

title: Why cosine shortens the force
md: Think of the arrow's shadow on the line. When the force lies along the line there is no tilt, $\cos 0° = 1$, and the whole force counts. Turn it to a right angle and the shadow vanishes. Cosine is the fraction of the force that survives the turn.

**Shown, a 50 N force:** at $60°$ to the line, $50\cos 60° = 50 \times 0.5 = 25$ N survives.
**At $90°$:** $50\cos 90° = 50 \times 0 = 0$: none of it acts along the line.

prompt: A force of 20 N acts at 60° to a straight line. What is its component along that line, in newtons?
explain: Half the force survives a turn of $60°$, as for the 50 N force above: $20\cos 60° = 20 \times 0.5 = 10$ N.

caption: The weight split down the slope and into it.

md: On a slope the useful directions are along the surface and at right angles to it, so the weight is the force to split. The angle between the weight and the line into the slope is the slope's own angle $\alpha$, so into the slope is $mg\cos\alpha$ and down the slope is $mg\sin\alpha$.

**Weight first:** $11 \times 10 = 110$ N.
**Down the slope:** $110\sin 30° = 55$ N; **into it:** $110\cos 30° = 95.26$ N.

prompt: A box of weight $W$ rests on a slope inclined at $\alpha$ to the horizontal. Which expression gives the component of the weight acting down the slope?
explain: The slope's angle sits between the weight and the line into the surface, so the cosine part goes into the slope and the sine part runs down it, as for the 11 kg box above.

text: 4. Which line the angle is measured from

alt: A box on a slope inclined at 21 degrees, pulled by a rope with a force of 75 N at 32 degrees to the slope itself. The slope's direction is continued as a dashed line from the box, and the 32 degree angle is marked between it and the rope.

caption: An angle given to the slope, not to the horizontal.

md: A question may give the angle to the horizontal, to the vertical, or to the slope itself. Only the angle between the force and the direction you are resolving along belongs in the cosine.

**Shown:** the rope is $32°$ from the slope, so along the slope it gives $75\cos 32° = 75 \times 0.848 = 63.60$ N.
**Not:** $32°$ from the horizontal, which would resolve along the wrong line.

title: Mechanics FM GCSE - Resolving Forces on Horizontal plane
why: Taught straight against this specification. Watch the angle being marked on the diagram before either ratio is chosen.

prompt: A rope pulls a box up a slope. The rope is at 32° to the slope, and the slope is at 21° to the horizontal. Which angle is used for the component of the pull along the slope?
explain: The component along the slope needs the angle between the rope and the slope, which the question gives directly as $32°$, as in the line above.

alt: A point O pulled by 36 N horizontally to the right and 14 N up and to the left at 60 degrees to the horizontal, with dashed reference lines through O.

caption: Two pulls whose horizontal parts face each other.

md: A component has a direction as well as a size. Choose one way along the line as positive; a component pointing the other way is then negative, and it is subtracted rather than added.

**Shown:** the 14 N pull gives $14\cos 60° = 7$ N to the left, which is $-7$ N.
**To the right in total:** $36 - 7 = 29$ N, not $36 + 7 = 43$ N.

prompt: A force of 16 N acts at 60° above the horizontal, to the left. Taking to the right as positive, which is its horizontal component?
explain: Its size is $16\cos 60° = 8$ N, and it points left, the negative way, as the 14 N pull did above: $-8$ N.

md: **An angle to the vertical** (2024, 2026). Now the vertical part is beside the angle, so it takes the cosine, and the horizontal part the sine.

**Shown:** 18 N at $25°$ to the vertical: vertically $18\cos 25° = 16.31$ N.
**Horizontally:** $18\sin 25° = 7.61$ N.

prompt: A force of P newtons acts at 30° to the vertical. Which expression gives its vertical component?
explain: Measured from the vertical, the vertical side is beside the angle, so it takes the cosine, as the 18 N force above did.

md: **A mass, not a weight** (2023, 2025). The question gives the mass; the weight $mg$ is what gets resolved. **Shown:** a 3 kg parcel on a 30° slope: $3 \times 10 = 30$ N first, then $30\sin 30° = 15$ N down the slope.

prompt: A crate of mass 12 kg rests on a slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal. What is the component of its weight acting down the slope, in newtons?
explain: Weight first, as for the parcel above: $12 \times 10 = 120$ N. Then $120\sin 30° = 60$ N down the slope.

md:
Split any force into a component along a line and one at right angles to it.
Resolve the weight on a slope into mg sine and mg cosine of the slope's angle.
Pick out which angle the question gives, and which line it is measured from.
Combine components that point opposite ways by subtracting.

Resolving is rarely asked for on its own: it sits inside 'Calculate the normal reaction' or 'Calculate the value of P', worth 2 to 4 marks. The first mark is for a correct resolved component written down; the last is for the value, to 2 decimal places. Stuck? Draw the right-angled triangle, mark the angle, and ask which side of it you want.
